How the tiers work
  • Top 10: ranks 1 to 10 on the final score among the players who qualify for ranking in this view.
  • Upper, Middle and Lower third: everyone else who qualifies, split into three equal groups by final-score rank. “Lower third” means he ranks in the bottom third of players who already qualified, not that he is a poor player overall.
  • Low sample: he does not qualify, so he has no rank and no tier. A player needs at least in this view. His rating is still shown, but with so few pressure balls it is pulled toward average and can mislead.
  • Each cell below says exactly which test he missed (or, for ranked players, his strongest and weakest part). Tiers compare a player only with others in the same discipline and view.

Problem statement: most reliable under pressure

Pressure = how much the next ball can swing the win probability (a win-probability model on balls left, wickets, runs needed and team strength; the top 20% of balls are high-pressure). Players are rated on runs above average per 100 pressure balls, adjusted for the batters or bowlers faced, the venue and batting role, then blended with consistency, run-rate arc (batters), a 0–10 Impact rating and match-shaping innings and spells. Pressure form is a weak signal in about 3.5 seasons of data, so every pick carries a stability figure. The step-by-step explanation below and its worked examples describe the “Both” view.

How the rating works, step by step

The short version. Every ball is worth the change it makes to the batting side’s chance of winning. We add those changes up, but only on the balls where the match could really swing (pressure balls). We compare each player with what an average player would have done against the same opponents, on the same ground, in the same role. We then reward players who do it every time, and we turn each innings into a football-style mark out of 10.

Step 1. What counts as pressure

A win-probability model looks at the match at every ball: balls left, wickets lost, runs needed and the required rate (in a chase) or the score (first innings), plus how strong the two teams are. It then asks: if this ball goes well or badly, how far could the win chance move? That number is the leverage of the ball. We call the top 20% of balls, by leverage, pressure balls.

  • A tight chase at the death (say 12 needed off 8, with wickets in hand): one ball can move the win chance by several points. Very high pressure.
  • A game that is already decided (the required rate is low and many balls remain, or the target is out of reach): no single ball changes much. Almost no pressure, so a six here earns almost nothing.
  • Early in the first innings: a single ball cannot decide the match, so powerplay balls are rarely high-pressure. The death overs carry about twice the pressure of any other phase.

Step 2. Points for every ball (how much a dot, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 or wicket is worth)

The points for a ball are the change in the batting side’s win probability, in percentage points. The batter gets those points, and the bowler gets the same amount with the sign reversed. So a dot is a loss for the batter and a gain for the bowler. The table below is the average value of each result in each situation, measured from every ball in the data. A positive number is good for the batter.

InningsPhaseDot1 run2 runs3 runs4 (and 5)6Wicket
First inningsPowerplay-0.01+0.19+0.41+0.45+0.82+1.25-7.64
First inningsMiddle-0.14+0.19+0.50+0.73+1.09+1.85-6.37
First inningsDeath-0.36-0.07+0.13+0.14+1.00+1.79-4.48
ChasePowerplay-0.69-0.05+0.56+1.36+1.84+3.19-7.34
ChaseMiddle-0.86-0.07+0.81+1.84+2.48+3.86-6.41
ChaseDeath-1.71-0.67+0.93+2.39+3.60+6.77-6.30

How to read it, in words:

  • Dot ball (0 runs): always a small loss for the batter, and it costs more as the match tightens. In a chase it costs 0.69 points in the powerplay, 0.86 in the middle and 1.71 at the death, about 2.5 times as much at the death as in the powerplay. Dots are a gold mine for the bowler for the same reason.
  • 1 run: roughly neutral early, but a loss late in a chase (a single at the death costs 0.67 points) because it does not keep up with the required rate.
  • 2 runs and 3 runs: small gains in the powerplay and middle, bigger at the death (a 3 at the death of a chase is worth +2.39).
  • 4 (and the rare 5): a clear gain everywhere, worth +3.60 points at the death of a chase against +1.84 in the powerplay.
  • 6: the biggest gain: +6.77 points at the death of a chase against +3.19 in the powerplay. When the game is already decided, the same six moves the win chance very little.
  • Wicket: the biggest loss for the batter, about 4 to 8 points depending on the situation, and the biggest gain for the bowler. A wicket by a batter who has already scored 15 or 30 does not cost any extra; the data showed no extra effect beyond the match situation. The slow start of the next batter is real (about 0.8 runs over the next 3 balls) and is already included in the 4 to 8 points.
  • Wides and no-balls count against the bowler. Dot-ball streaks: each extra consecutive dot adds a tiny extra cost (about 0.02 points).

Two quick examples at the death of a chase. A wild over: dot, 1, four, dot, six, wicket adds up to -0.03 points (almost nothing, because the dots and the wicket cancel the boundaries). A quiet over of three dots and three singles adds up to -7.16 points for the batter, which is about 7.2 points gained by the bowler, even though no wicket fell.

Step 3. The 0 to 10 match mark, the football way

Football analytics value every action by how much it changes the chance of scoring or winning, add the values up for the match, and then turn the total into a mark out of 10, judged against other players in the same position (6 is an average performance). We do the same: ball = action, win-probability points = its value, innings or spell = match.

  1. Add the points from the pressure balls of the innings (or spell). Only pressure balls count, so a quiet 40 in a dead game earns almost nothing, and a 12-off-4 balls cameo in a tight chase earns a lot.
  2. Compare that total with every other innings in the same position group: batting 1–3 (top order), 4–6 (middle order), 7 and below (lower order and finishers); bowling pace or spin, split by the phase where the spell’s pressure balls fell (powerplay, middle, death). A finisher is judged against finishers, and a death bowler against death bowlers.
  3. Mark = 6 + 1.25 × (how many standard deviations above or below the group average). An average pressure innings is a 6, a very good one is a 7 to 8, an outstanding one is a 9 to 10. A batter who only scores dots and throws his wicket gets only negative points and a mark below 6.

Points needed in a single pressure innings or spell for a given mark:

A player’s Impact rating is the average of his match marks, pulled toward 6 so that two lucky games cannot dominate.

Step 4. The main ranking rating (a fair comparison across players)

Win-probability points per ball are too noisy to rank players directly: a player’s total in one half of the data hardly predicted his total in the other half. So the main ranking rating uses a steadier version of the same idea, measured in runs above average per 100 pressure balls:

  • Every ball is compared with what an average player does in the same state (innings, over, wickets lost) and the same batting role. A dismissal is converted to runs (about 5.6 runs for a wicket, from the win-probability value of a wicket compared with a run).
  • Opposition and ground: batters and bowlers are estimated together, so a batter is credited for the bowlers he faced and a bowler for the batters he bowled to, with the ground allowed for.
  • Small samples: the rating is pulled toward average for players with few pressure balls. We tested whether a separate “clutch” skill exists beyond general quality: it does not predict better on held-out matches, so overall quality (adjusted for opposition) carries most of the rating and the pressure-specific part (uplift) gets a small weight.
  • Consistency: the share of his pressure innings, and of his seasons, that were above average. This rewards doing it every time, not one big night.
  • Run-rate arc (batters): in chases that start at a required rate of 9 or more, did the required rate fall between his walking in and leaving, compared with similar entries? Bringing it from 10 down to 7 or 8 is credited; letting it climb is not.
  • Match-shaping innings and spells (big moments): a 50 or a 100 in a big chase, or a 3-, 4- or 5-wicket spell, is worth a lot of win-probability points, and the model already counts those points ball by ball. On average a batting innings of 50–99 is worth about +12 points, a century about +24 (about +38 in a chase of 170 or more); a bowling spell with 3 wickets about +14, 4 wickets about +22 and 5 wickets about +22. We also count how often a player has an innings or spell worth 8 or more points (about one batting innings in eight), over all of his innings and spells, because that share is repeatable (rank correlation about 0.2 to 0.26 between halves of the data) and rewards the player who produces these moments regularly.
  • Extra credit rules inside match-shaping (added in this version): each of his innings or spells earns credit. Base: 1 point if it was worth 8 or more win-probability points. Match-best: +0.5 for the top scorer of the match (at least 20 runs; ties share) and +0.5 for 70 or more runs; for bowlers +0.5 for the most wickets in the match (at least 2) and +0.5 for 3 or more wickets. These two bonuses are halved when his team lost. Man of the match: +0.5, but only when that innings or spell was itself game-changing (8+ points), so a man-of-the-match award for a quiet contribution earns nothing. Knockouts: everything above is doubled in a final, qualifier or eliminator (24 such matches in the data). His value is the average credit over all of his innings or spells, pulled toward the league average when he has few. Check on repeatability (odd versus even and earlier versus later innings): for batters it rose from about 0.26 and 0.21 to 0.42 and 0.39, but part of that is role (openers and number threes top-score more often); for bowlers it fell slightly, from about 0.24 and 0.24 to 0.20 and 0.17, so for bowlers these bonuses add a little noise. The knockout part rests on only 24 matches.

Step 5. Putting it all together

Each component is converted to a standard score against the other ranked players and added with these weights:

  • Batters: pressure rating 38.5%, uplift 5.5%, consistency 11%, run-rate arc 15%, Impact rating 15%, match-shaping innings 15%.
  • Bowlers: pressure rating 49%, uplift 7%, consistency 14%, Impact rating 15%, match-shaping spells 15%.

The weights follow what held-out data supports: the pressure rating predicted later performance best, consistency and the Impact rating added weaker signals, the run-rate arc is highly repeatable and independent of the rating, and uplift adds the least. Only players with at least 120 pressure balls, 15 pressure innings and pressure balls in two seasons are ranked (90 batters and 88 bowlers); others show their rating but no rank.

IdeaIn football ratingsIn this cricket rating
An actionA pass, dribble, tackle, shot or loss of the ballOne ball: a dot, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, a wicket, a wide
Its valueHow much it changes the chance of scoring or winningHow much it changes the chance of winning (win-probability points)
A loss of the ballA bad touch or a misplaced pass costs valueA dot or a wicket costs value, more when the pressure is high
ContextA pass in the final third is worth more than one in defenceA six at the death of a tight chase is worth far more than a six in a dead game
Match markSum of action values, scaled to 0–10 against the player’s position (6 is average)Sum of pressure-ball points, scaled to 0–10 against the player’s position group (6 is average)
PositionGoalkeeper, defender, midfielder, forwardTop order 1–3, middle order 4–6, lower order 7+; pace or spin by phase
OppositionStrength of the opponent is allowed forBatters and bowlers estimated together; the ground allowed for
Over a seasonAverage rating and how often a player performsConsistency across innings and seasons, plus a small-sample correction
What is differentValues are often fixed from possession chainsValues come from a win-probability model of the match state, so the “pressure multiplier” is learned from data, not set by hand

One honest difference from football: our ranking rating is built on runs and wickets (a steadier measure) while the 0–10 mark is built on win-probability points. Both come from the same idea, and both are combined in the final score.

IPL and T20I together: how they are combined, and the single-competition views

IPL and national-team cricket are different (different opposition, conditions and quality), and the two never meet: IPL franchises do not play national teams. So the combination is built in three layers, and the switch at the top of the page lets you look at each competition alone.

  • Same definition of pressure, separate averages. The win-probability model is shared and has the competition as one of its inputs, with the strength gap between the two teams. But the “average ball” that every delivery is compared with is worked out inside each competition (by innings, over and wickets lost). An IPL death-over six is judged against IPL death overs and a T20I six against T20I death overs. A rating therefore means “better than the average for that competition”, not “better than a T20I average”.
  • One player, one set of ratings, when both are used. In the “Both” view, a player’s balls from both competitions feed one rating, so we assume his skill carries over from one to the other. Opposition is estimated from the balls in both competitions, but because the two sets of teams never face each other there is no direct bridge between them. Comparing an IPL-only player with a T20I-only player therefore rests on that assumption and on each competition’s own average.
  • Different quality of opposition. The T20I data includes associate nations, which are weaker on average. The team-strength gap in the win-probability model and the opposition adjustment partly allow for this, but not perfectly.
  • IPL only and T20I only. These views re-fit the whole model using only that competition’s balls. The pressure definition (the top 20% of balls by leverage) stays the same. Because each view has about half the data, only players with at least 80 pressure balls, 10 pressure innings and pressure balls in two seasons are ranked (against 120, 15 and two seasons in the combined view). Ranks and tiers differ between views, and a player with no balls in a competition does not appear in that view.

From raw data to the final lists

  1. The data. Ball-by-ball records of IPL and T20I matches since 2022: for every delivery the batter, bowler, runs, extras and any wicket, plus matches, playing XIs and squads. After scope rules we use 788 completed matches and 188,151 deliveries from the first and second innings. Left out: rain-affected matches with a revised target, abandoned and no-result games, super-overs, and A-team tournaments (Emerging Teams Asia Cup, Asia Cup Rising Stars). The data does not record bye and leg-bye runs, so these are approximated (byes 2, leg-byes 1); this only affects totals and targets.
  2. The state of the match at every ball: score, wickets lost, legal balls left, target and required rate in a chase.
  3. Win-probability model (one for the first innings, one for the chase), always tested on matches it was not trained on. On unseen matches its error is 0.212 in the first innings (0.250 for a model with no skill) and 0.132 in chases (0.249 for no skill).
  4. Pressure flag: the top 20% of balls by how far one ball can move the win chance.
  5. Points and match marks (Steps 2 and 3 above): win-chance points for every ball, summed on the pressure balls of each innings or spell, turned into a 0–10 mark within the player’s position group.
  6. Main rating (Step 4): runs above average per 100 pressure balls, adjusted for opposition, ground, role and small samples.
  7. Extras: consistency, the run-rate arc (batters) and the Impact rating.
  8. Score and rank: the weighted score (Step 5), ranked among players who have enough pressure balls (at least 120 pressure balls, 15 pressure innings and pressure balls in two seasons).
  9. Checks (below), then the final lists.

How we checked it

CheckWhat we didResult
Is pressure form a separate skill?Cross-validated on matches held out, scored on pressure balls onlyGeneral quality (adjusted for opposition, ground, role) cuts held-out error by about 0.5%; adding a free pressure-only effect, or up-weighting pressure balls, made predictions worse. So uplift gets a small weight.
Does the rating predict later play?Fit on the earlier half of matches (and odd-numbered matches), test on the later half (and even-numbered matches)Rank correlation with later overall performance: batters 0.27 and 0.31, bowlers 0.22 and 0.20. On later pressure balls alone the signal is weak (around 0 to 0.2) because the samples are small.
Is the run-rate arc repeatable?Odd versus even tough chase entriesRank correlation 0.65, and nearly independent of the main rating
Are big moments repeatable? (base flag only; the version with match-best, man-of-the-match and knockout credit is checked in Step 4)Share of innings (batters) or spells (bowlers) worth 8+ win-probability points, odd versus even and earlier versus laterRank correlation 0.26 and 0.21 for batters, 0.24 and 0.24 for bowlers. The average win-probability total per innings was much less repeatable for batters (0.08), which is why we use the share of big moments.
Do roles help?Role-based expectations against one league averageA small gain (about 0.1% lower held-out error) but the correct fairness adjustment
Ideas tested and not addedExtra value for a set batter, a big partnership, a wicket at the death, dot streaksNo extra effect beyond the match situation, except a tiny dot-streak effect (kept)
How stable are the lists?100 resamples of whole matches and 15 different settings (pressure cut-off, weights, shrinkage, eligibility, with or without arc and Impact)Batters: average chance of staying in the top 10 across 100 resamples: 49%; 5 of 10 stay in at least half of them; all ten are in the top 10 in at least 9 of 15 settings. Bowlers: average 60%; 7 of 10 stay in at least half of them; 10 of 10 are in the top 10 in at least 10 of 15 settings (the least secure is in 10).

How we reached the conclusion

  • Finding 1: overall quality, adjusted for who you faced, is the best guide to pressure performance. We could not find a separate “clutch” skill that predicts better than that.
  • Finding 2: pressure is concentrated in the death overs and in tight chases. A dot at the death of a chase costs about 2.5 times a powerplay dot; the same six is worth about twice as much at the death as in the powerplay.
  • Finding 3: the lists are therefore the players who combine the best opposition-adjusted quality on pressure balls with consistency across innings and seasons, the run-rate arc (batters) and a high Impact mark within their role.
  • How firm it is: the top of each list is stable under resampling and different settings; the lowest places are close calls. These are best estimates from about 3.5 seasons of data, not guarantees.

How pages 1 and 3 are built

  • Page 1, current squad: the squad listed on the Rajasthan Royals website, shown India-only by default. Each player is placed against every ranked player: Top 10, upper, middle or lower third, or “Low sample” if he lacks the 120 pressure balls, 15 pressure innings or two seasons needed for a rank. A low-sample player still shows his rating, but no rank.
  • Page 3, auction look-out: ranked players who are not in the squad, India-only by default. “Upgrade” means his score is higher than the squad’s best ranked Indian player in the same role. The “Why” column reads off his strongest components.
  • Nationality: taken from national-team appearances in the data and from the squad list. Players with only IPL franchise appearances are marked “India (inferred)” with a “?”; two ranked players (Sunil Narine and Faf du Plessis) were corrected by hand.
  • Not in the data: auction pool, contracts, prices and retentions. Availability at the auction is not checked.

Limits to keep in mind

  • Even the busiest players have only 120 to 600 pressure balls, so the intervals are wide.
  • The win-probability model knows the match state and team strength, not player quality or the pitch. A strong batter walking in makes a chase easier than the model assumes.
  • Roles are defined by batting position and bowler type and phase, not by the job given on the day.
  • Bye and leg-bye runs are approximated, so targets are accurate to within a few runs.
  • The run-rate arc credits team results when a batter finishes a chase.
  • Strengths of teams inside the IPL and inside T20I are estimated from 3.5 years of results; the two competitions are not compared directly.

Auction look-out

The page opens with the Top 10 only: the best 10 batters and best 10 bowlers by score among players not in the Rajasthan Royals squad. Change “Show” to “Show every match” to see everyone, ranked and low-sample players both. Filter by availability (no IPL 2026 team, or in another IPL team), tier, discipline, nationality and role, and sort any column. “Upgrade” means the score is higher than the squad’s best Indian player in the same role. The data has no auction pool, so availability only means “in no IPL 2026 squad list I could read”. Low-sample players have no score or rank, so they sit at the bottom of a score sort.

Auction plan

The decision

The release list and the first reason for each release are the team’s own call (price and results). The data columns beside them come from the pressure model in the view selected at the top. Prices (in ₹ crore) are not in the match data. They come from the Rajasthan Royals site (auction buys) and a pre-auction retention list (retained players), and are not in the pressure model. Dasun Shanaka and Emanjot Chahal: no price found. Purse left is ₹16.05 crore before the auction minus ₹13.40 crore spent, about ₹2.65 crore (the Rajasthan Royals site gives the first two figures; one other site lists ₹1.10 crore). Purse after releases adds the released players’ prices back as a simple sum. The real purse for the next auction follows the league’s retention rules, so treat it as an estimate.

Finishers: Hetmyer’s role

What this page lists
  • Every batter in the data who has faced at least 30 balls at number 5 or lower, the finisher slots. Pakistan players are left out.
